title: Equality, anti-racism and advocacy for women made vulnerable
blurb: Apply the Equality Act, read the inequality data, and advocate for women whose care is at risk of being unequal.
question: On day 3 after birth, Abena, a Black British woman, says she feels breathless with chest pain. A colleague says she is 'just anxious, like a lot of these mums'. What should the midwife do?

teach.h: Fair is not the same as identical
teach.body: Formally, the Equality Act 2010 protects nine characteristics, prohibits discrimination, harassment and victimisation, and requires reasonable adjustments for disabled people. The Code asks midwives to treat people fairly and without discrimination (20.2) and to challenge discriminatory attitudes and behaviour (3.4). In plain English: give every woman the care she needs, which sometimes means more, different or earlier care, and speak up when bias creeps in.

teach.caption: s17: treating a woman unfavourably because she is breastfeeding within 26 weeks of birth is pregnancy and maternity discrimination.

teach.text: NICE NG194 (2021) quotes older MBRRACE figures: Black women 4 times more likely to die. The current 2022-24 data brief says NEARLY THREE times. Both show a stark disparity; use the current figure.

teach.body: Section 20 has three requirements: change a provision, criterion or practice; remove or avoid a physical feature; and provide an auxiliary aid, such as information in an accessible format. The disabled person must not be charged (s20(7)). NG235 1.4.8 adds: use independent interpreters, including British Sign Language and Makaton, and healthcare passports for people with learning disabilities or autistic people.

Midwife Sam hears Abena describe breathlessness and chest pain, both signs NG194 says need advice without delay because they may be VTE, the leading cause of maternal death. Sam challenges the 'just anxious' remark, records Abena's own words and escalates for urgent medical review. Her oximeter reads 96%, but Sam remembers that pulse oximeters may overestimate saturations in darker skin (NG255 1.4.9) and does not let the number falsely reassure.

steps.sub: Name the remark, refocus on her

steps.label: Escalate
steps.sub: Urgent review if signs are serious

items: Nine protected characteristics, including pregnancy and maternity; s17 covers breastfeeding for 26 weeks.
Direct, indirect, harassment and victimisation are all unlawful; adjustments for disability must be free.
MBRRACE 2022-24: Black women nearly 3 times, most deprived areas about twice, the maternal death rate.
Avoid assumptions (Code 1.3); challenge discriminatory remarks (Code 3.4); escalate red flags.
Know where clinical tools can mislead in darker skin.

summary: You can now apply the Equality Act to maternity care, describe current MBRRACE disparities accurately, and make reasonable adjustments. You can also recognise and challenge bias and advocate for a woman whose symptoms are being dismissed.

A.q: Which of the following is a protected characteristic under section 4 of the Equality Act 2010?
options: Socio-economic status
Pregnancy and maternity
Immigration status
Body mass index
A.why: Pregnancy and maternity is one of the nine protected characteristics listed in s4.

whyNot.0: Deprivation drives inequality, but socio-economic status is not a s4 characteristic.
whyNot.2: Immigration status is not a protected characteristic, although race (including nationality) is.
whyNot.3: BMI is not a protected characteristic, though weight should be discussed sensitively.

A.q: According to the MBRRACE-UK data brief for 2022-24, how did the maternal death rate for Black women compare with that for White women?
options: About four times higher
About twice as high
Nearly three times higher
No significant difference
A.why: The 2022-24 data brief reports a nearly three-fold difference (risk ratio 2.72).

whyNot.0: Four times was the older 2020 figure quoted in NICE NG194, not the current one.
whyNot.1: About twice describes the gap between the most and least deprived areas.
whyNot.3: The difference for Black women was statistically significant.

A.q: Nadia, who is Deaf and uses British Sign Language, attends her booking appointment. Which is the most appropriate adjustment?
options: Book a qualified BSL interpreter at no cost to her
Ask her partner to sign the conversation for her
Write all questions down for her to read and answer
Ask her to bring a relative who signs to each visit
A.why: Section 20 requires auxiliary aids without charge, and NG235 1.4.8 calls for independent interpreters, including for BSL.

whyNot.1: A partner is not an independent interpreter and may prevent private disclosure.
whyNot.2: Written English may not be her first language; BSL is her preferred language.
whyNot.3: Relatives are not independent and confidentiality is compromised.

B.q: A midwife hears a colleague say a woman's labour pain is exaggerated 'because women from her culture always make a fuss'. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Note the comment and raise it at the colleague's appraisal
Agree to delay analgesia until labour is confirmed
Reassure the colleague privately that no harm was meant
Challenge the remark and focus on the woman's own account
B.why: Code 3.4 asks midwives to challenge discriminatory attitudes, and Code 1.3 to avoid assumptions. NG235 1.6.2: pain is expressed differently, including by culture.

whyNot.0: Waiting for appraisal leaves the bias affecting care now.
whyNot.1: Delaying pain relief on a stereotype is discriminatory care.
whyNot.2: Excusing the remark does not protect the woman or change practice.

B.q: An antenatal clinic sends appointment letters in English and discharges any woman who misses two visits. Women who cannot read English are discharged far more often. Which form of discrimination is this most likely to be?
options: Direct discrimination
Indirect discrimination
Harassment
Victimisation
B.why: Indirect discrimination (s19): a practice applied to everyone that puts people sharing a protected characteristic, here race, at a particular disadvantage.

whyNot.0: Direct discrimination is less favourable treatment because of the characteristic itself.
whyNot.2: Harassment is unwanted conduct that violates dignity or creates a hostile environment.
whyNot.3: Victimisation is detriment because someone did a protected act, such as complaining.

B.q: After a caesarean, Folake, who has dark skin, has a respiratory rate of 24 and a pulse of 118. Her oximeter reads 95%. What should the midwife bear in mind about this reading?
options: A clear pleth waveform shows the reading is accurate
The oximeter may overestimate her saturations
The reading confirms she is not deteriorating
Readings are more reliable in darker skin tones
B.why: NG255 1.4.9: pulse oximeters may overestimate oxygen saturation in people with darker skin, so a normal-looking reading must not falsely reassure.

whyNot.0: A good trace does not remove the overestimation reported in dark skin, which can hide hypoxia (NG255 1.4.9).
whyNot.2: Her respiratory rate and pulse are raised and need acting on whatever the oximeter shows.
whyNot.3: NICE warns the opposite: accuracy is reduced in darker skin.

C.q: Abena, 3 days after birth, reports breathlessness and chest pain. A colleague says she is anxious and suggests a relaxation leaflet. What is the most appropriate initial action?
options: Escalate for urgent medical review for possible VTE
Offer reassurance and an anxiety self-help leaflet
Repeat her observations in 4 hours and then review
Refer her to the perinatal mental health team
C.why: NG194 1.2.4: breathlessness or chest pain after birth needs advice without delay as possible VTE, the leading cause of maternal death in MBRRACE 2022-24.

whyNot.1: Attributing symptoms to anxiety without assessment risks missing a fatal VTE.
whyNot.2: A 4-hour delay is unsafe for possible pulmonary embolism.
whyNot.3: Mental health referral is not the priority before physical causes are excluded.

C.q: An NHS trust is reviewing its maternity services under the public sector equality duty (s149). What does the duty require?
options: Providing identical services to every woman
Recruiting staff to match local ethnic groups
Due regard to equality of opportunity
Recording the religion of every woman booked
C.why: Section 149 requires public authorities to have due regard to eliminating discrimination, advancing equality of opportunity and fostering good relations.

whyNot.0: Identical services can entrench inequity; the duty is about due regard, not sameness.
whyNot.1: The PSED does not set recruitment quotas.
whyNot.3: Data collection may help, but the duty itself is due regard to the three aims.

C.q: Kerry, 22, has a learning disability and is discussing place of birth. Her support worker says Kerry 'won't understand' and should be booked at the obstetric unit. What should the midwife do?
options: Accept the support worker's view, as she knows Kerry best
Book the obstetric unit and explain the plan afterwards
Ask the consultant obstetrician to decide in her best interests
Adapt the information, such as Easy Read, and support Kerry to decide
C.why: Capacity is presumed and all practicable steps must be taken to help her decide (MCA s1). NG235 1.4.8 supports adapted communication such as healthcare passports.

whyNot.0: A support worker cannot make the decision, and capacity must not be assumed absent.
whyNot.1: Deciding for her without support breaches her autonomy.
whyNot.2: Best interests applies only once a lack of capacity is established, not assumed.

reteach.title: Same destination, different routes
reteach.question: If two women need to reach the same safe outcome, why might one need a different route?

blocks.body: Equality law and the Code aim for the same safe outcome for every woman. Because of disability, language, racism or deprivation, some women need a different route: an interpreter, more time, an adjusted policy, or a midwife who listens harder. Giving everyone the identical route can leave some women behind.

blocks.text: Equal treatment does not mean identical treatment: the s20 duty exists precisely because sameness can disadvantage disabled people.

explain.body: Nine protected characteristics (s4). Unlawful conduct includes direct discrimination (s13), discrimination arising from disability (s15), indirect discrimination (s19), harassment (s26) and victimisation (s27). Pregnancy and maternity discrimination in services includes breastfeeding within 26 weeks of birth (s17).

test.q: A woman complains about her care. Afterwards, staff make her wait longer than others for postnatal checks. Which form of prohibited conduct is this?
options: Indirect discrimination
Harassment
Victimisation
Direct discrimination
test.why: Victimisation (s27) is subjecting someone to a detriment because they did a protected act, such as making a complaint.

whyNot.0: Indirect discrimination involves a general rule disadvantaging a group.
whyNot.1: Harassment is unwanted conduct violating dignity linked to a characteristic.
whyNot.3: Direct discrimination is treatment because of a protected characteristic, not a complaint.

explain.body: Three requirements (s20): adjust a provision, criterion or practice; deal with a physical feature; provide an auxiliary aid, including accessible formats (s20(6)). No charge to the person (s20(7)). Record the need, not just the diagnosis (Accessible Information Standard).

test.q: A woman with a visual impairment needs her birth plan information in large print. Who pays for this adjustment?
options: The woman, at cost price
The woman's GP practice
The maternity service provider
A charity chosen by the woman
test.why: The service provider makes the adjustment, and s20(7) prohibits passing the cost to the disabled person.

whyNot.0: The disabled person must not be charged (s20(7)).
whyNot.1: The duty sits with the service providing the information.
whyNot.3: The provider cannot shift its legal duty onto a charity.

explain.body: MBRRACE-UK 2022-24: 12.80 maternal deaths per 100,000 maternities. Black women nearly 3 times the rate of White women; the most deprived fifth of areas about twice the least deprived; women 40 and over almost 3 times those aged 25-29. VTE leads deaths in pregnancy and 6 weeks after; suicide leads from 6 weeks to a year.

test.q: A student says deprivation makes 'little difference' to maternal death. Which MBRRACE 2022-24 finding corrects this?
options: Most deprived areas have about twice the rate
Most deprived areas have about four times the rate
Deprivation affects neonatal but not maternal deaths
Deprivation matters for women over 40 but not others
test.why: Women in the 20% most deprived areas of England had a maternal mortality rate about twice that of the least deprived (risk ratio 1.94).

whyNot.1: Four times is not the deprivation figure in the data brief.
whyNot.2: The data brief shows a clear deprivation gradient in maternal deaths.
whyNot.3: The deprivation gap applies across the population, not one age band.

explain.body: Advocate for women made vulnerable by physical, psychological, social, cultural or spiritual circumstances (SPM 1.16). Avoid assumptions based on culture, ethnicity or religion (CG110 1.3.9; Code 1.3). Challenge discriminatory attitudes (Code 3.4) and escalate concerns (Code 16.1).

test.q: At handover, a midwife hears that a Roma woman 'won't come back anyway, so don't bother arranging follow-up'. What is the best response?
options: Accept it, as attendance has been poor
Arrange follow-up and challenge the assumption
Ask the woman to arrange her own follow-up
Leave follow-up for the GP to arrange later
test.why: Assumptions based on ethnicity breach Code 1.3 and CG110 1.3.9. The midwife should challenge the remark (Code 3.4) and adapt care to help her attend.

whyNot.0: Acting on a stereotype denies her care she is entitled to.
whyNot.2: Shifting responsibility to her ignores barriers to access.
whyNot.3: Passing the task on avoids the midwife's own responsibility and delays care.
